study.title: Differential Modulating Effect of Acupuncture in Patients With Migraine Without Aura: A Resting Functional Magnetic Resonance Study
study.study_design: Single-arm intervention study with matched healthy controls; resting-state fMRI obtained at three timepoints in migraine group and one timepoint in healthy controls; 6 weeks acupuncture treatment followed by 24 weeks follow-up
study.population: Patients with migraine without aura recruited from neurology outpatient clinic or acupuncture clinic; matched healthy controls recruited by advertisements
study.inclusion_criteria: age 18–65 years, right-handedness, 2–8 migraine attacks during the past month, diagnosis of migraine at least 6 months earlier, no prophylactic headache medications during the past month, no psychoactive or vasoactive agents during the past 3 months, no history of acupuncture, and ability to provide informed consent; for HCs: right-handed, matched for age and education level, normal neurological examination
study.exclusion_criteria: other type of primary or secondary headache, history of a clinically significant disorder, pregnancy or breast-feeding, contraindications to MRI or acupuncture, severe head deformity, and intracranial lesions

arms.dropouts: 3 patients lost to follow-up; 3 patients with MwoA excluded because of excessive head movement during scanning
1 HC excluded because of excessive head movement during scanning

interventions.stimulation_type: acupuncture with electroacupuncture at selected points
interventions.anatomical_location_exact: head (DU20, EX-HN5, GB20, GB8, GB5, GB15), hand (LI4), foot (LR3)
interventions.laterality_exact: bilateral for GB20, GB8; not_reported for other points
interventions.penetration_exact: needle inserted to achieve the Deqi sensation
interventions.manipulation_exact: needles inserted to achieve the Deqi sensation; electric stimulation applied at GB20 and GB8 bilaterally
interventions.deqi_intended_exact: yes; needles inserted to achieve the Deqi sensation
interventions.electrical_intensity_exact: varied from 0.1 to 1.0 mA until the patient felt comfortable
interventions.practitioner_description_exact: Two licensed acupuncturists administered all the acupuncture treatments
interventions.participant_instructions_exact: All patients agreed not to take any regular medications for migraine for the duration of the study. In the event of severe pain, ibuprofen (as 300-mg sustained-release capsules) was allowed as rescue medication.
interventions.treatment_rationale_given_exact: Acupoints were selected according to the Chinese guidelines for acupuncture in patients with migraine and those used in previous randomized controlled trials. A migraine attack is usually unilateral and related to the circulation of the gallbladder meridian of foot Shaoyang.

extraction_notes.note: No sham acupuncture or active control group was included. The paper explicitly states this as a limitation: 'it did not include a control group that received sham acupuncture or medication, which meant that the superiority of acupuncture and the specificity of the acupoints used could not be confirmed.'
Expectancy, credibility, and blinding success were not measured or reported in this study. No instrument was used to assess these constructs.
Deqi sensation was stated as intended but no quantitative data on sensory responses during or after acupuncture were reported. No MASS or other deqi scale was used.

Patients were not followed up by fMRI scans during the follow-up period (weeks 7-30). Therefore, persistent changes in ReHo and their correlation with maintained clinical efficacy could not be assessed.

The n_total_analyzed_neuroimaging was stated as 37 patients and 15 HCs; however, fMRI data for MwoA patients included 34 patients at the third scan (3 were excluded due to head movement after first scan). The ANOVA within-subjects analyses therefore used n=34 for the MwoA group; between-group comparisons used 37 patients and 15 HCs at baseline.

The paper reports 'P < 0.05, FWE-corrected at the cluster level' for the between-group comparison (Table 3A), but reports 'P < 0.001, GRF, cluster P < 0.05, cluster >20' for the within-group ANOVA. These are different threshold approaches. The post-hoc comparisons use 'FWE, P < 0.05'. All thresholds are preserved as reported.
No specific adverse event counts or participants affected were reported despite stating that adverse events were recorded at each treatment session.

The Table 2 p-values column header states 'P-value for pairwise comparison VS baseline' and 'VS treatment', but the reported values (<0.001) appear to reflect the overall ANOVA F-test result rather than specific pairwise comparisons. The exact pairwise test used is not described beyond 'one-way ANOVA' with post-hoc structure.

The between-group comparison (PM < HC) used 37 patients and 15 HCs at baseline, but Table 3A caption does not specify n. The neuroimaging section states 'fMRI data for 37 patients and 15 HCs were included in the analysis', so n=52 total for this comparison was used.
The paper does not state a PMID. The DOI 10.3389/fneur.2021.680896 was extracted directly from the paper.

The correlation analysis between ReHo and clinical outcomes was performed using Pearson/Spearman but the paper does not specify which test was used for which correlation (only 'Pearson/Spearman correlation' stated). The reported r values are presented as correlation coefficients.
Duration of migraine for HCs is listed as '/' in Table 1 (not applicable). Mean duration of migraine for patients was 16.19 (12.81) years.
